title: What is cardinality explosion in Prometheus metrics (a separate time series per unique label-value combination, so an unbounded/high-cardinality label — userId, orderId, email, full URL / path with IDs, trace id — multiplies series into the millions), what incident does it cause (TSDB OOM / crashed Prometheus / failed scrapes / slow dashboards), and how do you avoid it (keep labels low-cardinality and bounded, put high-cardinality identifiers in LOGS/traces not metric labels, aggregate before exposing, apply relabel/limit rules)?
shortTitle: Cardinality explosion in Prometheus metrics — what it is, the incident it causes, and how to avoid it
topicTitle: What is cardinality explosion in Prometheus metrics (a separate time series per

s1_definition.profdef: Cardinality explosion is the uncontrolled growth of time-series in Prometheus caused by attaching a high-cardinality or unbounded label to a metric. Because Prometheus creates one distinct time-series for every unique combination of metric name and label values, a label whose value space is large or infinite — a user id, order id, email, trace id, or a URL path containing ids — multiplies the series count into the millions. The result is memory exhaustion in the time-series database, crashed or OOM-killed Prometheus, failed scrapes, and slow or unloadable dashboards.
s1_definition.analogy: Prometheus keeps one notebook page for every unique kind of measurement. A sensible label is like "transaction type" — there are only a few values (transfer, deposit, withdrawal), so only a few pages. But imagine someone decides to label every measurement with the customer's account number. The National Bank of India has millions of customers like Rajesh SAV2001 and Priya CUR3001, so Prometheus now needs millions of pages, one per account, forever — even for accounts that transacted once and never again. The notebook grows until the supervisor's desk collapses under its weight. That collapse is cardinality explosion: Prometheus runs out of memory, crashes, and stops monitoring the whole bank.
s1_definition.oneliner: One time-series per unique label combination means an unbounded label like account id or trace id explodes series into the millions and crashes Prometheus — keep those identifiers in logs and traces, never in metric labels.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cardinality explosion is the uncontrolled growth of time-series in Prometheus caused by attaching a high-cardinality or unbounded label to a metric. Because Prometheus creates one distinct time-series for every unique combination of metric name and label values, a label whose value space is large or infinite — a user id, order id, email, trace id, or a URL path containing ids — multiplies the series count into the millions. The result is memory exhaustion in the time-series database, crashed or OOM-killed Prometheus, failed scrapes, and slow or unloadable dashboards.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Prometheus keeps one notebook page for every unique kind of measurement. A sensible label is like "transaction type" — there are only a few values (transfer, deposit, withdrawal), so only a few pages. But imagine someone decides to label every measurement with the customer's account number. The National Bank of India has millions of customers like Rajesh SAV2001 and Priya CUR3001, so Prometheus now needs millions of pages, one per account, forever — even for accounts that transacted once and never again. The notebook grows until the supervisor's desk collapses under its weight. That collapse is cardinality explosion: Prometheus runs out of memory, crashes, and stops monitoring the whole bank.

**One line to remember:** One time-series per unique label combination means an unbounded label like account id or trace id explodes series into the millions and crashes Prometheus — keep those identifiers in logs and traces, never in metric labels.

sections.s2_technical:
The root mechanic is that Prometheus identifies a time-series by its full label set. The metric `transfers_total{service="transfer", status="success"}` is a different series from `transfers_total{service="transfer", status="failure"}`. The total number of series for a metric is the product of the number of distinct values of each label. If a metric has a `service` label with five values and a `status` label with three values, that is fifteen series — fine. But if you add an `account_id` label with two million values, you now have five times three times two million, which is thirty million series. Each series carries overhead in memory for its index and its recent samples, so millions of series exhaust RAM.

High-cardinality labels are the ones with large or unbounded value spaces. The classic offenders are user id, customer or account id, order or transaction id, email address, session id, trace id, request id, and a full URL path that embeds an id such as `/accounts/SAV2001/transactions/TXN-99817`. Each unique request creates a brand new series that lives essentially forever, because Prometheus keeps series around even after they stop receiving samples, until a long retention window passes. Even bounded-looking labels can be dangerous at scale: a label combining region times instance times endpoint times status can multiply faster than you expect.

The incident this causes is severe and cascading. As series count climbs, Prometheus memory grows until the process is OOM-killed or the node runs out of RAM. When Prometheus restarts, it tries to replay its write-ahead log, which is now huge, so startup is slow or fails. Scrapes begin to fail because the ingestion path is saturated. Dashboards that run aggregations over millions of series become slow or time out. In the worst case you lose all monitoring precisely when you need it most. A single bad deploy that adds one unbounded label can take down the entire monitoring stack.

Avoiding it is about discipline and guardrails. First, keep labels low-cardinality and bounded by design — labels should be things with a small, stable set of values like service name, environment, status code class, HTTP method, or region. Second, put high-cardinality identifiers where they belong: account ids, transaction ids, and trace ids go into logs and traces, not metric labels. A log line can hold the account id and the trace id for the one request; a metric should only hold the aggregate. Third, aggregate before exposing — instead of a per-account counter, expose a per-account-type counter. Fourth, apply guardrails in Prometheus itself: `metric_relabel_configs` can drop or rewrite dangerous labels at scrape time, a `sample_limit` on a scrape job caps how many series a single target can produce, and you can set `label_limit` and `label_value_length_limit`. Fifth, monitor your own cardinality with queries like `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` and `count(count by (le)(...))` to find which metric is exploding.

A senior nuance: the fix for an already-happening explosion is to drop the offending label at scrape time with relabeling, redeploy the instrumentation to stop emitting it, and if needed delete the bad series from the TSDB. The preventive culture is a rule in code review: any new metric label must have a provably bounded value set, and anything that looks like an id goes to logs or traces. Histograms also quietly add cardinality through their `le` bucket label, so you keep bucket counts reasonable.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service exposes a metric for transfer counts. A well-meaning engineer adds an `account_id` label so they can "see each customer's activity on the dashboard."

Problem 1 — With the account_id label, every one of the bank's millions of accounts — Rajesh SAV2001, Priya CUR3001, and millions more — creates its own time-series. The series count explodes and Prometheus memory climbs toward an OOM crash. This is the cardinality explosion itself.

Problem 2 — The team needs to detect this before it crashes production. They compute the number of distinct series the metric would produce and compare it to a safe budget.

Problem 3 — The fix is to remove the account_id label from the metric (keeping it in logs and traces instead) and keep only a low-cardinality account_type label (savings, current). This collapses millions of series down to a handful.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `MetricSeriesStore` that creates a new series for each unique label combination, a `CardinalityGuard` that rejects a label set whose projected series count exceeds a budget, and a demo that first shows the explosion with account_id and then the safe version with account_type. Classes: `LabelSet`, `MetricSeriesStore`, `CardinalityGuard`, and a `CardinalityDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — Prometheus guardrails against cardinality

```yaml
# prometheus/prometheus.yml — cap series and drop dangerous labels at scrape time
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'transfer-service'
    metrics_path: '/actuator/prometheus'
    sample_limit: 10000                   # scrape fails safely if a target emits >10k series
    label_limit: 15                       # reject targets with too many labels
    label_value_length_limit: 128
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['transfer-svc:8080']
    metric_relabel_configs:
      # DROP any high-cardinality account_id label before it reaches the TSDB
      - source_labels: [account_id]
        action: labeldrop
        regex: 'account_id'
      # Collapse URL paths with embedded IDs into a bounded route template
      - source_labels: [path]
        target_label: path
        regex: '/accounts/[^/]+/transactions/[^/]+'
        replacement: '/accounts/:id/transactions/:id'
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer metric design decision — first with an account_id label, then redesigned with an account_type label — against a cardinality budget of one thousand series.

Step 1: The guard evaluates the bad design. With two million accounts and two status values, the projected series count is four million, which vastly exceeds the budget of one thousand. The guard rejects it and names account_id as the offending high-cardinality label, advising that it belongs in logs or traces.

Step 2: The simulation fills a model TSDB with per-account series to make the growth visible. As it crosses one hundred thousand series, a warning fires that memory is climbing. After three hundred thousand distinct account series, the store logs that Prometheus is heading for an out-of-memory crash — this is the explosion made concrete.

Step 3: The guard evaluates the good design. By dropping account_id and keeping only a bounded account_type label with two values, the projected series count collapses to four, which is comfortably within budget, so the guard approves it.

Step 4: The account id and the amount for the specific transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 are emitted as a log line carrying the trace id, which is the correct home for high-cardinality detail. Monitoring survives and per-request detail is still available via logs and traces.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cardinality explosion is what happens when you attach a high-cardinality or unbounded label to a Prometheus metric. Prometheus creates one separate time-series for every unique combination of a metric name and its label values, and the total series count is the product of the distinct values of each label. So a label like status with three values is harmless, but a label like account id, user id, order id, email, or trace id has millions of possible values, and multiplying that across your other labels produces millions of series, each consuming memory essentially forever because Prometheus keeps series around long after they stop receiving samples.

The incident this causes is severe and cascading. Memory in the time-series database climbs until Prometheus is out-of-memory killed. On restart it has to replay a huge write-ahead log, so it comes back slowly or not at all. Scrapes start failing, dashboards that aggregate over millions of series time out, and you lose your monitoring exactly when you need it most. A single deploy that adds one unbounded label can take down the whole monitoring stack.

Avoiding it is about discipline and guardrails. I keep metric labels low-cardinality and bounded by design — service name, environment, HTTP method, status code class, region — things with a small stable set of values. Anything that looks like an identifier goes into logs and traces, not metric labels, because a log line is the right place to record an account id and a trace id for a single request. I aggregate before exposing, so instead of a per-account counter I expose a per-account-type counter. And I put hard guardrails in Prometheus itself: a sample_limit on the scrape job so a misbehaving target fails safely instead of taking down the server, metric_relabel_configs to drop a dangerous label at scrape time, and self-monitoring queries that find which metric is exploding. In my project at the National Bank of India, an engineer once added an account_id label to the transfer counter, which would have created a series for every one of millions of accounts like Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001. We caught it against a cardinality budget, dropped the label with relabeling, kept only a bounded account_type label of savings or current, and moved the account id and amount into the logs and traces where they belong. The principle I always state is that metrics are for bounded aggregates and identifiers belong in logs and traces.
